verses.text: Hear the word which Yahweh speaks to you, house of Israel!
Yahweh says, “Don’t learn the way of the nations, and don’t be dismayed at the signs of the sky; for the nations are dismayed at them.
For the customs of the peoples are vanity; for one cuts a tree out of the forest, the work of the hands of the workman with the ax.
They deck it with silver and with gold; they fasten it with nails and with hammers, that it not move.
They are like a palm tree, of turned work, and don’t speak: they must be carried, because they can’t move. Don’t be afraid of them; for they can’t do evil, neither is it in them to do good.”
There is no one like you, Yahweh. you are great, and your name is great in might.
Who should not fear you, King of the nations? For it belongs to you. Because among all the wise men of the nations, and in all their royal estate, there is no one like you.
But they are together brutish and foolish, instructed by idols! It is just wood.

There is silver beaten into plates, which is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz, the work of the artificer and of the hands of the goldsmith; Blue and purple are their clothing; they are all the work of skillful men.
But Yahweh is the true God; he is the living God, and an everlasting King. At his wrath, the earth trembles, and the nations are not able to withstand his indignation.
“You shall say this to them: ‘The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth, these shall perish from the earth, and from under the heavens.’”
He has made the earth by his power. he has established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding has he stretched out the heavens.

when he utters his voice, there is a tumult of waters in the heavens, and he causes the vapors to ascend from the ends of the earth. He makes lightnings for the rain, and brings the wind out of his treasuries.
Every man has become brutish and without knowledge; every goldsmith is disappointed by his engraved image; for his molten image is falsehood, and there is no breath in them.
They are vanity, a work of delusion. In the time of their visitation they will perish.
The portion of Jacob is not like these; for he is the former of all things; and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance: Yahweh of Armies is his name.
Gather up your wares out of the land, you who live under siege.
For Yahweh says, “Behold, I will sling out the inhabitants of the land at this time, and will distress them, that they may feel it.”
Woe is me because of my injury! My wound is serious: but I said, “Truly this is my grief, and I must bear it.”
My tent is destroyed, and all my cords are broken. My children have gone away from me, and they are no more. There is no one to spread my tent any more, and to set up my curtains.
For the shepherds have become brutish, and have not inquired of Yahweh. Therefore they have not prospered, and all their flocks are scattered.
The voice of news, behold, it comes, and a great commotion out of the north country, to make the cities of Judah a desolation, a dwelling place of jackals.
Yahweh, I know that the way of man is not in himself: it is not in man who walks to direct his steps.
Yahweh, correct me, but in measure: not in your anger, lest you bring me to nothing.

Pour out your wrath on the nations that don’t know you, and on the families that don’t call on your name: for they have devoured Jacob. Yes, they have devoured him and consumed him, and have laid waste his habitation.

footnotes.content: Jeremiah opens with the prophet's own urgency: listen. The word Yahweh speaks isn't whispered—it's meant to be heard by the whole house, to shake them awake. I've learned that when the Lord calls us to listen, He's about to show us something we're missing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't learn the way of the nations—don't be swept into their customs or their panics. Jeremiah warns against imitating the fears of the godless. I notice how fear spreads like contagion, especially from those who have no anchor in the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The customs of peoples are vanity—hollow. Jeremiah points to a common sight: a tree cut, carried, crafted. It starts in the forest, nothing special, but human hands are about to make it something they'll bow to. That's how idolatry begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Silver, gold, nails, hammers—all the craft and wealth of a nation poured into holding up what cannot stand on its own. I see how much effort we waste propping up what was never meant to be held up.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Like a palm tree of turned work, beautiful but mute, paralyzed, carried rather than walking. These idols are decorative helplessness dressed as hope. Jeremiah's message is blunt: don't fear them. They can't move, can't speak, can't do anything but stay still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There is no one like you, Yahweh. After naming the vanity of made things, Jeremiah turns the gaze upward. The contrast is electric—contrast is worship. You are great. Your name carries the weight of might itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Who should not fear you, King of the nations? This is the fear that sets us free—not trembling dread of wooden things, but reverence before the One who actually holds all nations. Among the wise men and the royal courts, there is no one like Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Together brutish and foolish, instructed by idols—it's just wood. Jeremiah strips the glamour away. No matter how many powerful voices teach us to bow before emptiness, the verdict stands: foolishness and wood. The shame of it should break our hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Silver beaten into plates from Tarshish, gold from Uphaz—Jeremiah names the trade routes, the exotic sources, the finest craftsmen. He's showing how far we'll go, how much we'll spend, to craft our own gods. The world's most skilled hands, lavished on lies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But Yahweh is the true God, the living God, the everlasting King. After the parade of human effort and empty beauty, 'But'—that one word opens the door to reality. He alone is true. He alone lives. He alone will outlast kingdoms and the things they carved.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth shall perish from the earth—a strange, haunting sentence. Tell this to them, Jeremiah says. Gods made by human hands will be unmade. Only the Maker endures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He has made the earth by his power—established the world by wisdom, stretched out the heavens by understanding. These are the fingerprints of God: power, wisdom, understanding. Not gold or silver. The very structure of creation speaks to His nature.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When he utters his voice, there is tumult of waters in the heavens—lightning, rain, wind from his treasuries. Jeremiah shows me a God who commands the weather itself, who speaks and the elements obey. What idol could match that?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every man has become brutish and without knowledge—the craftsman included. The goldsmith who carves an engraved image is disappointed by his own work. There's a sadness here: the maker knows the falsehood, feels the emptiness of the thing he's made.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They are vanity, a work of delusion. When the time of visitation comes, they will perish. Jeremiah doesn't say they might disappoint—he says they will vanish. The reckoning is sure. What we build outside the Lord cannot stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The portion of Jacob is not like these. After the catalogue of hollow things, Jeremiah turns back to the covenantal reality: Jacob's portion is the Lord Himself. Yahweh of Armies—the tribe of His inheritance. We are His inheritance, not the other way around.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gather up your wares out of the land, you who live under siege. The oracle shifts from condemnation of idolatry to a command—prepare for what's coming. Judah is besieged. It's time to pack what matters and abandon what doesn't.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I will sling out the inhabitants of the land at this time, and will distress them, that they may feel it. God's judgment is real and unavoidable—He will sling them out like stones from a sling. The distress is meant to bring them to their senses.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Woe is me because of my injury—the prophet's own heart breaks for his people. He speaks their pain, bears it with them. Jeremiah doesn't stand apart preaching; he weeps with Jerusalem, grieves her destruction as his own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: My tent is destroyed, all my cords are broken. My children have gone away from me. Jeremiah speaks the complete desolation—shelter gone, bonds severed, the next generation scattered. This is the exile in a single verse: homelessness and separation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The shepherds have become brutish and have not inquired of Yahweh—the leaders stopped listening. When pastors cease to seek the Lord's face, their flocks scatter. Spiritual decay always starts with abandonment of prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The voice of news, a great commotion out of the north country—the Babylonian invasion comes with a sound first, then the devastation. Judah will be desolate, a dwelling place of jackals. That's how swiftly blessing becomes ruin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I know that the way of man is not in himself. After speaking judgment and exile, the prophet turns inward in humility. The deepest truth: I cannot direct my own steps. That awareness should drive us to the One who can.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh, correct me, but in measure, not in your anger. Readers today hear an echo of this cry whenever we face discipline—the prayer for correction to restore us, not to destroy us. Even in judgment, the faithful ask for mercy's hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pour out your wrath on the nations that don't know you and don't call on your name. The chapter closes with a prayer that the judgment fall on the wicked, not on Jacob. It's a plea for justice, a cry that God's covenant people not be confused with those who refuse Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
